113.title: The partly column
113.hook: modern writers, not Epictetus, add a third column: things partly up to me
113.howItsDone: Some modern readers of Stoicism use a three-column sort, following William Irvine: what's fully up to me, what isn't, and what's partly up to me, which they break down until they find the piece that is fully theirs.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the archer, who does everything to aim well and lets the wind have the rest. Your line was aim, then let go.

Try Epictetus's two columns on a real worry, and something awkward happens. Say you're worried about your health. Is it up to you? Not entirely: genes, accidents, luck. Not up to you at all? That doesn't feel right either. You choose what you eat, whether you walk, whether you see a doctor. Or your kid's grades. Your marriage. Your job. Plenty of what people actually lie awake about doesn't fit neatly in either column. It sits somewhere in between. Modern writers noticed, and some of them drew a third column.
screen: `YOUR HEALTH: MINE?` → `NOT ENTIRELY. NOT NOT.` → `A THIRD COLUMN.`

segments.voice: First, the honest history. Epictetus had two columns, not three. The third was added in modern times, notably by the American philosophy professor William Irvine in a 2009 book on Stoic practice. He called it the trichotomy of control: things we have complete control over, things we have no control over, and things we have some control over. Some Stoic scholars push back. Epictetus didn't need a third column, they say, because anything partly up to you can be split into the part that's yours and the part that isn't. Here's the useful thing: follow either path carefully and you end up in the same place. Take the tennis match, Irvine's own example. Winning is partly up to you; you can't control your opponent, the wind or the line judge. So you break the partly column open and look for the piece that's fully yours: to practice hard, and play as well as you can today. That becomes your goal. Not win, but play my best. Which is exactly Cato's archer from yesterday, aiming well and letting the result go. The partly column isn't a place to leave things. It's a place to open them up. Your health: the walk, the vegetables, the appointment are yours; the rest is not. Your kid's grades: the quiet desk, the encouragement, the patience are yours; the grades are theirs. Find your part. Do your part. Let the rest be the rest.
screen: `EPICTETUS HAD TWO COLUMNS.` · `IRVINE, 2009: A THIRD.` · `BREAK IT OPEN.` · `FIND THE PIECE THAT'S FULLY YOURS.` · then, large: `MY PART ONLY.`

segments.voice: Hold one thing you care about that's partly up to you, your health, a relationship, a project, and break it open: what, in this, is fully mine? Maybe one call, one habit, one kind word, one hour; name it clearly. Then set the rest down beside it, gently, not mine, and breathe with your part in your hands.
Trichotomy. William Irvine's name for the third column, what's partly up to you, broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Today's word.
Your line: my part only. Even big, tangled things have a piece that's yours. Day one hundred thirteen, done.

114.title: Serenity, courage, wisdom
114.hook: a twentieth-century prayer by Reinhold Niebuhr asks for serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart
114.howItsDone: Some Christians pray the Serenity Prayer, and Alcoholics Anonymous and other recovery groups often say it aloud together at the close of a meeting.

segments.voice: Yesterday: trichotomy, the partly column broken open to find the piece that's fully yours. Your line was my part only.

You may have seen it on a kitchen magnet, or a plaque in a hospital waiting room, or hanging on the wall of a church basement where folding chairs are set out in a circle. A short prayer, three lines long, said aloud in rooms like that one. In one breath, it says much of what Epictetus has been teaching all week. But it comes from no ancient Stoic. It comes from a twentieth-century American Christian.
screen: `A KITCHEN MAGNET.` → `A CHURCH BASEMENT CIRCLE.` → `THREE LINES, SAID ALOUD.`

segments.voice: The prayer is usually credited to Reinhold Niebuhr, an American Protestant theologian who taught in New York. Scholars have argued about its origins, but the best evidence points to Niebuhr using it in sermons and talks from the early 1930s on. It asks God for three gifts. Serenity, to accept the things that cannot be changed. Courage, to change the things that can. And wisdom, to know the one from the other. Later, Alcoholics Anonymous took it up, and in AA and other recovery groups it is often said aloud together at the close of a meeting. Lay it beside this week. Epictetus drew two columns: up to us, not up to us. The prayer asks for a strength for each. For the not-mine column, serenity: not giving up, but setting down. For the mine column, courage, because the things you can change are often the ones you're afraid to touch: the hard conversation, the first meeting, the apology. Then the third gift, which may be the hardest: wisdom to know the difference. That's the sorting itself. Epictetus draws the line cleanly on the page; in a real week, finding it takes work. For the people who pray it, this is a prayer to God, and the gifts come from God. Nobody's prayer gets rewritten here. I only notice that a Christian theologian and a Stoic teacher, many centuries apart, stood at a similar crossroads, and both said it takes wisdom to choose the road.
screen: `REINHOLD NIEBUHR, THE 1930s.` · `SERENITY, COURAGE, WISDOM.` · `A STRENGTH FOR EACH COLUMN.` · `THE HARDEST GIFT IS THE SORTING.` · then, large: `KNOW THE DIFFERENCE.`

segments.voice: Not a new prayer, just plain words about your own life: bring one situation to mind and finish three sentences inside, the part of this I can't change is, the part I can change is, the way I'll tell them apart is. If you pray, you can say the prayer itself, in the words you know.
Serenity. Calm acceptance of what can't be changed, the first of three gifts in Niebuhr's prayer. Today's word.
Your line: know the difference. Serenity for one column, courage for the other. That's day one hundred fourteen.

115.title: Other people's opinions
115.hook: what others think is on their side of the line; how we treat them is on ours (Enchiridion 1)
115.howItsDone: People who practice Stoicism often treat reputation as not up to them, following Enchiridion 1, and turn their attention to their own judgments and how they treat others.

segments.voice: Yesterday: serenity, courage, and the wisdom to tell them apart. Your line was know the difference.

You post a photo and check it again, and again, before the hour is up. You say something in a meeting and spend the evening replaying the face your colleague made. A relative says at dinner, so you're still doing that job? And it rattles around your head for a week. Other people's opinions of you: you try hard to steer them, and have very little grip on them. Epictetus put them on his list, and his line runs right through the middle of the dinner table.
screen: `CHECKED AGAIN, AND AGAIN.` → `THE FACE IN THE MEETING.` → `STILL DOING THAT JOB?`

segments.voice: Go back to the Handbook's first lines. On the not-up-to-us list, right after the body and property, Epictetus puts reputation: what other people think and say of us. On the up-to-us list, first of all, he puts our own opinions and judgments. That's the line. Their opinion of me: their side. My opinion, and what I do next: my side. Marcus Aurelius noticed how odd this is. He wonders, in the Meditations, how each of us loves ourselves more than anyone else, and yet cares more about what others think of us than what we think of ourselves. Epictetus adds a sharp practical point elsewhere in the Handbook. If someone speaks badly of you, don't defend yourself; answer, in paraphrase, that they clearly didn't know your other faults, or they'd have mentioned those too. It's a joke, and it's also freedom. The line has two sides, and the second matters as much as the first. Their opinion is theirs to think. But how you treat them is yours. Letting go of what someone thinks is not the same as not caring about them. You can let your relative's comment stay theirs, and still pass the potatoes warmly, still ask how their knee is. It's easier, in fact: when you stop trying to win their verdict, your hands are free to be kind. And if the criticism has something true in it, that's yours to use, quietly, without needing them to see you do it.
screen: `REPUTATION: NOT UP TO US.` · `MARCUS: WE LOVE OURSELVES MOST.` · `THEY DIDN'T KNOW MY OTHER FAULTS.` · `HOW I TREAT THEM IS MINE.` · then, large: `THEIRS TO THINK.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one opinion someone holds of you that bothers you, a comment, a look, a silence, and notice where you feel it in your body. On an out-breath, picture handing it back across the table: that's yours to think. Then ask if anything in it is true and useful; keep that small piece, and set the rest down.
Enchiridion. Epictetus's Handbook, where he puts their opinion of you on their side of the line, and how you treat them on yours. Today's word.
Your line: theirs to think. How you treat them stays yours. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

116.title: The body is on loan
116.hook: Epictetus lists even the body among things not fully ours (Enchiridion 1)
116.howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat the body as not fully theirs, following Enchiridion 1 and 11: they care for it steadily and try to meet illness and aging without outrage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Enchiridion, their opinion on their side of the line. Your line was theirs to think.

A friend lends you her car for the weekend, and something changes in the driver's seat. The fries stay in the bag. The mirrors get checked twice. The tank goes back full, maybe after a trip through the car wash. Nobody asked for any of it. A borrowed thing gets a different kind of care. Now a strange thought from Epictetus, the last of our week on control: what if your body is more like the borrowed car than one you own?
screen: `A FRIEND'S CAR.` → `NO FRIES, MIRRORS TWICE.` → `WHAT IF THE BODY IS BORROWED?`

segments.voice: Go back to the first lines of the Handbook: some things are up to us, some are not. The very first thing on the not-up-to-us list is the body. That sounds wrong. My body is the most mine thing there is. But look at it the way Epictetus did. You didn't choose its height, or its genes, or when it catches a cold. You can't order your knee to stop hurting or your hair to stay. It ages on its own schedule. You live in it, you steer it, you're responsible for it. But you don't fully command it. Later in the Handbook, he gives the picture that goes with this. Never say of anything, I have lost it, he says, in paraphrase; say instead, I have given it back. What we have is given for a time, like a traveler's room at an inn: use it well while you're there, and don't pretend it's yours forever. Here's the surprise. This isn't a reason to neglect the body. It's the reason to care for it well. The borrowed car gets the careful driving. Sleep, water, a walk, the vegetables, the checkup: not vanity, and not punishment. That's how a good guest treats a borrowed thing. And the loan helps with the other side too. When the knee hurts or the mirror shows a new gray hair, you can meet it with less outrage. That part was never yours to command. What's yours is how you care for it, and how you meet what it does.
screen: `FIRST ON THE NOT-MINE LIST: THE BODY.` · `YOU STEER IT; YOU DON'T COMMAND IT.` · `NOT LOST: GIVEN BACK.` · `CARE FOR IT LIKE A BORROWED THING.` · then, large: `ON LOAN.`

segments.voice: Move your attention slowly through the body, feet, legs, belly, chest, hands, shoulders, face, and look it over the way you'd look over a borrowed car: with interest, not judgment. Where is it tired, and where does it ache? Then ask what one thing a good guest would do for it, water, sleep, a stretch, a walk, and breathe with that choice.
Handbook. Epictetus's book, where the body is listed among things not fully ours, which is why it deserves careful keeping. Today's word.
Your line: on loan. From mine or not mine to on loan, the week's six lines all ask the same question. A new week, on gratitude, starts tomorrow.

117.title: Three good things
117.hook: writing three good things each night was linked to more happiness in a 2005 study (Seligman et al.), with modest effects
117.howItsDone: The three good things exercise is widely used in positive psychology courses and therapy: each night for a week or longer, people write three things that went well that day and why each happened.

segments.voice: Yesterday Epictetus closed our week on control: even the body is borrowed. Your line was on loan.

Here's something your brain does without asking. At the end of the day, it hands you a summary, and the summary is biased. The rude driver makes the highlights. So does the late bus. The perfectly fine lunch, the stranger who held the door, the song you liked on the radio: cut for time. Psychologists call this lean toward the bad the negativity bias, and it's probably kept our ancestors alive. But it doesn't make for a fair report. A new week, on gratitude, starts with an exercise simple enough to seem silly.
screen: `THE BRAIN'S DAILY SUMMARY.` → `THE RUDE DRIVER MAKES IT.` → `THE HELD DOOR DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: In 2005, the psychologist Martin Seligman and his colleagues at the University of Pennsylvania ran an online study of several simple exercises. In one, every night for a week, you write down three things that went well today, and for each one, why it happened. No journal, no ritual. Three things and a reason. Compared with a placebo exercise, writing about early memories, the three good things group reported being a bit happier and a bit less depressed. Here's the surprise: the difference was still showing six months later, especially in people who kept doing it on their own. Now, the honest part. The effects were modest. Later studies have found smaller, mixed results, and nobody should expect a nightly list to fix a hard life. It isn't a cure, and gratitude forced on someone in pain can hurt; that comes back later this week. But the exercise does something clever. It works directly against the bias. The brain's summary cuts the good bits; this puts them back in. And the second half, why did it happen, matters. It makes you notice the causes: that you asked for help, that a friend thought of you, that you went outside. Good luck becomes something you can see, and sometimes repeat. Many traditions teach gratitude as a duty or a prayer. This one is a small experiment anyone can run, on the back of a receipt.
screen: `SELIGMAN, 2005.` · `THREE THINGS, AND WHY.` · `MODEST, BUT LASTING.` · `PUTTING THE GOOD BITS BACK.` · then, large: `THREE GOOD THINGS.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day and find one thing that went well; small counts, a good coffee, a text, a moment of quiet. Ask why it happened, and stay with it a breath or two. Then find a second, and a third, each with its why.
Seligman. The psychologist whose study had people write three things that went well each night, and why. Today's word.
Your line: notice why it happened. Three things and a reason, nothing more. Day one hundred seventeen, done.

118.title: Counting blessings
118.hook: Emmons and McCullough (2003) found weekly gratitude lists brought small lifts in wellbeing
118.howItsDone: Some therapists and wellbeing courses use gratitude lists, often a few things written once a week, drawing in part on Emmons and McCullough's 2003 studies.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Seligman's study, three good things, and why each one happened. Your line was notice why it happened.

Count your blessings. Grandmothers say it, usually across a kitchen table. There's an old gospel hymn with that title from 1897. It's said so often it can sound like a way of telling someone to stop complaining. So in the early 2000s, two psychologists decided to find out whether it actually does anything. They took the grandmother's advice and put it into a study with a control group.
screen: `COUNT YOUR BLESSINGS.` → `GRANDMOTHERS AND HYMNS.` → `PUT TO THE TEST.`

segments.voice: They were Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough, and their 2003 paper was called Counting Blessings Versus Burdens. In the first study, college students were split into three groups. Once a week, for ten weeks, one group wrote down up to five things they were grateful for. A second wrote five hassles, the irritations of the week. A third simply wrote five events that had affected them. At the end, the gratitude group felt better about their lives as a whole and more hopeful about the week ahead, and they reported fewer physical complaints. They even said they'd spent more time exercising. Later studies in the same paper, including one with people living with neuromuscular disease, found similar small lifts. That word small matters: modest changes, not transformations. What's interesting is the comparison. Nobody gave the hassles group harder weeks; they just spent their attention on the burdens. The gratitude group spent the same few minutes on the blessings. Same life, same week, different count. The grandmother was right about one thing and wrong about another. Counting doesn't make problems go away. But what you count is what you notice, and what you notice starts to shape the story you tell about your life. And the first study was weekly, not daily: a few minutes once a week was enough to show a difference.
screen: `EMMONS AND McCULLOUGH, 2003.` · `BLESSINGS, HASSLES, EVENTS.` · `SMALL LIFTS, NOT MIRACLES.` · `WHAT YOU COUNT IS WHAT YOU NOTICE.` · then, large: `COUNT THEM.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last seven days, not just today, and find one thing you're grateful for: a person, a meal, a moment of rest, something that didn't go wrong. Hold it for a breath, then find a second, a third, up to five. If you get stuck, that's fine; stay with the ones you found, and breathe with the list.
Counting blessings. A weekly list of what you're grateful for, which brought small lifts in wellbeing in the Emmons and McCullough studies. Today's word.
Your line: count them. The grandmother had a point, if not the whole point. See you tomorrow.

119.title: Thank them directly
119.hook: a gratitude letter read aloud gave one of the biggest short-term lifts in early studies
119.howItsDone: The gratitude visit, writing a letter to someone never properly thanked and reading it to them, is used in positive psychology courses and therapy, following Seligman and colleagues' 2005 study.

segments.voice: Yesterday: counting blessings, five from the week. Your line was count them.

Somewhere in your past is a person who changed your life and was never properly thanked. A teacher who saw something in you. A neighbor who drove you to the hospital. A coach, an aunt, a friend who stayed on the phone until 3am. It's easy to tell other people about someone like that. Telling them is another matter. For two days the thanks stayed inside you, on a list. Today it goes somewhere.
screen: `THE TEACHER WHO SAW YOU.` → `NEVER PROPERLY THANKED.` → `TODAY IT GOES SOMEWHERE.`

segments.voice: In the same 2005 study that tested three good things, Martin Seligman's team tried another exercise, the gratitude visit. You write a letter to someone who was especially kind to you but was never properly thanked. Then you deliver it in person and, if you can, read it aloud to them. Of all the exercises in that study, this one gave the biggest boost in happiness in the short run, a clear jump right after the visit. The lift held for about a month, then faded: a single gratitude visit is a big wave, not a new tide. A later study, by Amit Kumar and Nicholas Epley, found something else. Asked to predict how the person would feel getting their letter, the writers guessed too low. They expected it to be awkward, or not to matter much. The people receiving the letters were more pleased, and less awkward, than the writers predicted. The researchers suggest this misjudgment may keep people from saying thanks at all. So the research adds a push to do it on purpose, in words, with some detail. Not thanks for everything: what exactly they did, and what difference it made. Detail is what makes a thank-you land. And it doesn't have to be a long letter. Three honest lines, said to them, count.
screen: `THE GRATITUDE VISIT.` · `THE BIGGEST SHORT-TERM LIFT.` · `WE GUESS TOO LOW.` · `WHAT THEY DID, AND WHAT IT CHANGED.` · then, large: `SAY IT TO THEM.`

segments.voice: Let one person come to mind, someone you've never properly thanked, and picture their face. In your head, shape three lines: what they did, what it changed for you, and what you want them to know now. Keep each one simple and true.
Epley. The researcher who found people guess too low about how much a thank-you letter will mean, a push to say it anyway. Today's word.
Your line: say it to them. Detail over drama: what they did, what it changed. That's day one hundred nineteen.

screen: `DAY 119 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: GRATITUDE WITHOUT THE FORCED SMILE.`

people tend to underestimate how much a thank-you note will mean
in one study, receivers were more pleased, and less awkward, than writers predicted.
a good thank-you should be vague and general
detail makes it land: what they did, and what difference it made.

fork.setup: you've written a thank-you letter to an old teacher. it feels awkward, and you're sure it won't mean much to them. what do the studies suggest?
options: skip it: it'll just be awkward.
keep it for yourself instead.
send it: they'll likely be more pleased than you expect.
fork.reveal: writers guess too low. in Kumar and Epley's study, receivers were more pleased, and less awkward, than predicted.

trapdoor: what you thought: saying thanks is just good manners.
what it means: a thank-you said to someone directly, with detail, which lifted happiness more than any other exercise in one early study.
what a scholar hears: Kumar and Epley, Psychological Science, 2018, found letter writers underestimate how surprised and pleased recipients will be.

sources.ref: Seligman, Steen, Park and Peterson, American Psychologist 60, 2005 (the gratitude visit)
Kumar and Epley, "Undervaluing gratitude: expressers misunderstand the consequences of showing appreciation," Psychological Science 29, 2018
